item.title: Impression, Sunrise
item.lesson: In 1874, a group of young painters rejected by the official Salon staged their own exhibition in a photographer's studio on the Boulevard des Capucines. Monet showed this quick harbor view of his hometown, Le Havre at dawn — an orange sun over water, mist swallowing the ships, painted in perhaps a single sitting. Needing a title, he said, 'put Impression.' The critic Louis Leroy pounced, titling his mocking review 'Exhibition of the Impressionists' and jeering that wallpaper was more finished. The insult stuck, was adopted with pride, and named the most beloved movement in art history. The painting shows exactly what the revolution was: not the harbor, but the seeing of the harbor — atmosphere, reflection, a moment of light that will not survive the next five minutes. In 1985 armed thieves stole it from the Marmottan; it was recovered five years later in Corsica, the fame of art's most consequential title having made it impossible to sell.
item.lookFor: Cover the sun with your thumb and the picture nearly dissolves into gray-blue fog — then release it and watch the single orange disk, and its broken reflection, reassemble the entire scene. Monet's whole career is in that trick.
